sentences.text: Vouivria was a herbivorous sauropod dinosaur belonging to the family Brachiosauridae that lived in what is now France during the Late Jurassic.

The holotype specimen of Vouivria is a partial skeleton that lacks the skull, though it includes numerous elements such as neck and back vertebrae, ribs, shoulder blades, forelimb bones, pelvic bones, and leg bones.
This animal is estimated to have reached a body length of fifteen meters and a weight of fifteen tonnes.
The femur, or thighbone, of Vouivria measures 146 centimeters in length.
The third metacarpal features a unique ridge that splits into a bulge near the top quarter of the bone when held vertically.
The fourth metacarpal possesses a flange along the top third of its inner rear corner.
Two transverse ridges run between the lower condyles of the femur at the border with the rear shaft.
Well-formed laminae on the front underside and rear underside of the transverse process distinguish the front tail vertebrae of Vouivria from its closest relatives.
The humerus has a deltopectoral crest that doubles in transverse width as it extends downward.
The genus name Vouivria is derived from a French legend of a winged dragon or wyvern known as la vouivre.
If correct, Vouivria could be the oldest known brachiosaurid and the oldest member of the Titanosauriformes.
Workers discovered large fossil bones at a chalkstone quarry near Damparis, France, in April 1934.
The excavation of the Vouivria skeleton began in May 1934 and concluded on June 22, 1934.
The genus Vouivria and its type species V. damparisensis were formally named and described in 2017 by Philip D. Mannion, Ronan Allain, and Olivier Moine.
The species name damparisensis refers to the animal's origin in Damparis.
Evidence suggests Vouivria died near a coastal lagoon, was scavenged by theropods, and was subsequently buried by a new chalk layer that preserved its bones.
Seven theropod teeth found among the bones were assigned to Megalosaurus insignis.
Phylogenetic analysis places Vouivria as a basal member of the Brachiosauridae, positioned between Europasaurus and Brachiosaurus altithorax.
Albert-Félix de Lapparent originally considered the specimen to belong to the family Brachiosauridae.
Vouivria lived approximately 163.5 to 157.3 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic.
The holotype was found in the Calcaires de Clerval formation, likely in the Tidalites member of Mouchard, dating to the middle to late Oxfordian stage.
